summary.text: Take \(p=13\): the relevant symbols are \((3/13)=1\), \((2/13)=(5/13)=-1\), and \((-1/13)=1\), while \(13=3\cdot1^2+10\cdot1^2\); moreover, every integer representation \(13=3x^2+10y^2\) forces \(x^2=1\). Thus the claimed third-case residue is \(2\cdot13-12=14\pmod{169}\), but direct evaluation of the finite sum gives \(S(13)\equiv138\pmod{169}\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the conjecture by considering the prime \(p=13\) and the third of its five cases.

For integers \(b,c\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\), write
\[
T_k(b,c)=[X^k](X^2+bX+c)^k.
\]
To obtain a term of degree \(k\), one must choose \(i\) copies of \(X^2\), \(i\) copies of the constant \(c\), and \(k-2i\) copies of \(bX\). Consequently
\[
T_k(b,c)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
 \binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}c^i.
\]
Thus the sum appearing in the conjecture is the integer
\[
S(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81).
\]

We first check that \(p=13\) satisfies all the hypotheses of case (3). Clearly, \(13\) is prime and \(13>7\). Moreover,
\[
13=3\cdot 1^2+10\cdot 1^2,
\]
so it has the representation required in that case.

The relevant quadratic-character conditions also hold. In the notation of the OEIS statement,
\[
\left(\frac{13}{3}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=1.
\]
The nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(13\) are
\[
1,3,4,9,10,12.
\]
In particular, \(2\) is not a square modulo \(13\), and hence
\[
\left(\frac{2}{13}\right)=-1.
\]
Also, the nonzero squares modulo \(5\) are \(1\) and \(4\), while \(13\equiv3\pmod 5\). Therefore
\[
\left(\frac{13}{5}\right)=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)=-1.
\]
Finally, \(-1\equiv12\pmod {13}\) is a square, for example \(5^2\equiv12\pmod {13}\), so
\[
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)=1.
\]
Thus all three character assumptions in case (3) are satisfied. Equivalently, if the conditions are written with \((3/13)\) and \((5/13)\), as in the formalized version, their values are again \(1\) and \(-1\): \(3\) belongs to the displayed list of squares modulo \(13\), whereas \(5\) does not.

We next note that the conjectured right-hand side is independent of the choice of representation of \(13\) by \(3x^2+10y^2\). Indeed, suppose that integers \(x,y\) satisfy
\[
13=3x^2+10y^2.
\]
Both terms on the right are nonnegative. Hence \(10y^2\le 13\), so the integer square \(y^2\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). It cannot be \(0\), since that would give \(3x^2=13\). Therefore \(y^2=1\), and substitution gives
\[
3x^2=13-10=3,
\]
whence
\[
x^2=1.
\]
Thus every integral representation in this case has \(x^2=1\).

It remains to compute \(S(13)\) modulo \(13^2=169\). The following table performs this finite computation. In each row, all entries after \(k\) are reduced modulo \(169\). The columns labeled \(T_2\) and \(T_{14}\) mean \(T_k(2,81)\) and \(T_k(14,81)\), respectively; \(C\) means \(\binom{2k}{k}\); and the last two columns give the product forming the \(k\)-th summand and the running sum.
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r|r}
k&T_k(2,81)&T_k(14,81)&\binom{2k}{k}&
\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81)&\text{running sum}\\ \hline
0&1&1&1&1&1\\
1&2&14&2&56&57\\
2&166&20&6&147&35\\
3&135&84&20&2&37\\
4&6&91&70&26&63\\
5&38&45&83&139&33\\
6&162&102&79&40&73\\
7&112&129&52&91&164\\
8&150&65&26&0&164\\
9&14&22&117&39&34\\
10&23&164&39&78&112\\
11&166&45&26&39&151\\
12&116&142&156&156&138
\end{array}
\]
Every entry in the two \(T\)-columns follows directly from
\[
T_k(b,81)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
\binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}81^i,
\]
and the summand column is then obtained by multiplying its three preceding entries modulo \(169\). Thus the final entry in the running-sum column proves
\[
S(13)\equiv138\pmod {169}.
\]
For completeness, evaluation over the integers before reduction gives
\[
S(13)=244652768223970439760599585455536537025,
\]
and division by \(169\) leaves remainder \(138\), consistently with the table.

On the other hand, case (3) of the conjecture predicts, for any representation \(13=3x^2+10y^2\),
\[
S(13)\equiv
\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)(2\cdot13-12x^2)
\pmod {13^2}.
\]
We proved above that \(x^2=1\) for every such representation, and we also found \(({-1}/13)=1\). Therefore the conjectured residue is
\[
1\cdot(26-12)=14\pmod {169}.
\]
But the actual residue is \(138\), and
\[
138-14=124
\]
is not divisible by \(169\). Hence
\[
S(13)\not\equiv14\pmod {169}.
\]

Thus \(p=13\) satisfies every hypothesis of case (3), including the required integral representation, but its asserted congruence is false. Since the conjecture claims that all five stated conclusions hold for every prime \(p>7\), this single counterexample disproves Conjecture 3 for A336982.
